title: Using Modules
description: Bring in ready-made code from Python's built-in modules with import.

content.value: You do not have to build everything from scratch. Python arrives with a large pile of ready-made code, sorted into modules, and each module is a collection of tools for one job. Bringing one in takes a single line at the top of your file.

import random

dice = random.randint(1, 6)
print("You rolled a", dice)

After the import, you reach a tool by writing the module's name, a dot, then the tool's name. Without the import the name `random` means nothing at all, and Python stops with a `NameError`. Switch the import off in the explorer below to see exactly that.

The `random` module is what you reach for when a program should not do the same thing every time: rolling dice, shuffling a deck, picking a prize. `randint(a, b)` gives a whole number between the two, including both ends, and `choice()` picks one item out of a list.

import random

print(random.randint(1, 6))                       # 1 to 6, either end possible
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))
`randint(1, 6)` includes 6, unlike `range(1, 6)`, which stops at 5. The two look alike and behave differently, so it is worth reading twice.

The everyday operators cover most arithmetic. The `math` module covers the rest: square roots, rounding in a chosen direction, and stored values such as pi. Note that `math.pi` is a value rather than a function, so it takes no parentheses.

import math

print(math.sqrt(25))     # 5.0, always a float
print(math.pi)           # 3.141592653589793
print(math.floor(4.8))   # 4, rounded down
time, and Another Way to Import
The `time` module can pause your program, which is handy for letting a countdown land one line at a time instead of all at once.

import time

print("Starting...")
time.sleep(1)
print("One second later!")

There is a second form of import that pulls one tool out of a module by name. You then use it on its own, without the module name in front. It is shorter, but the module name is a useful reminder of where a tool came from, so use it for the handful of tools you call constantly.

from random import randint

print(randint(1, 6))   # no random. in front this time

editorCode:
import random
import math

print("Dice roll:", random.randint(1, 6))
print("Pick one:", random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))
print("Square root of 81:", math.sqrt(81))
print("Rounded down:", math.floor(9.7))

quiz.question: Which keyword brings a module into your program?
quiz.explain: import loads a ready-made module so you can use its tools without writing them yourself.

quiz.question: What happens if you call random.randint(1, 6) without importing random first?
quiz.explain: Until the import line runs, the name random does not exist, so Python has no idea what you are referring to.

quiz.question: Which of these can randint(1, 6) never return?
quiz.explain: randint includes both ends, so 1 and 6 are both possible. 0 is outside the range entirely.
